parole.testo: Internationalism derived from English electrode, coined by British scientist Michael Faraday in 1833, first used in his Diary (laboratory notebook) from the Ancient Greek words ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”) (from which the word electricity is derived) and ὁδός (hodós, “way”).

parole.significato: empathy (intellectual identification of the thoughts, feelings, or state of another person)
parole.testo: From English empathy, a twentieth-century borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐμπάθεια (empátheia, literally “passion”) (formed from ἐν (en, “in, at”) + πάθος (páthos, “feeling”)), coined by Edward B. Titchener to translate German Einfühlung. The modern Greek word εμπάθεια (empátheia) has an opposite meani

From English epistemology, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστήμη + λόγος (epistḗmē + lógos). Due to suffix ־לוגיה, the word is also a perfect cognate with Slavic equivalents: Russian эпистемология (epistemologija), Polish epistemologia, etc.
Borrowed from English arachnophobia, arachno- + -phobia, from Ancient Greek ἀράχνη (arákhnē, “spider”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). By surface analysis, אָרַכְנוֹ (arakhno) + ־פוֹבְּיָה (-fobya).

parole.significato: a graph (an ordered pair in graph theory)
parole.testo: From English graph, ultimately from Ancient Greek γράφω (gráphō, “to scratch, to scrape, to graze”).
Internationalism derived from English diode, coined by William Eccles in 1919, after Ancient Greek δίοδος (díodos). For the suffix, compare אלקטרודה (elektróda, “electrode”).
Borrowed from English hedonism, from Ancient Greek ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”) + -ism.

parole.significato: hedonist (someone devoted to the pursuit of pleasure)
parole.testo: Borrowed from English hedonist, from Ancient Greek ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”) + -ist.

parole.significato: A homograph: a word with the same spelling but different meaning.
parole.testo: Borrowed from English homograph and cognates in other European languages; ultimately from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Homosexual, gay, same-sex; said of a person, animal, relationship, trait, etc.
parole.testo: From English homosexual and cognates in other European languages. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ὁμός (homós) and Latin sexus. By surface analysis, הוֹמוֹ־ (homo-) + ־סֶקְסוּאָלִי (-seksu'áli).

parole.significato: Heterosexual, straight, opposite-sex, male-female; said of a person, animal, relationship, trait, etc.
parole.testo: From English heterosexual and cognates in other European languages. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἕτερος (héteros) and Latin sexus. By surface analysis, הֵטֵרוֹ־ (hetero-) + ־סֶקְסוּאָלִי (-seksu'áli).

catena.termine: τῆλε (“far away, afar”) + πάθος (“condition, disease, state”)

parole.testo: Borrowed from English telepathy, derived from Ancient Greek τῆλε (“far away, afar”) + πάθος (“condition, disease, state”).

From various European cognates such as English method, ultimately from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, “pursuit of knowledge, investigation, mode of prosecuting such inquiry, system”), from μετά (metá, “after”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way, motion, journey”).

parole.significato: a polygon (a plane figure bounded by straight edges)
parole.testo: Internationalism, from English polygon and cognates in other European languages. Ultimately from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”). By surface analysis, פּוֹלִי־ (poli-) + גוֹן.
From English colossus, ultimately from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós).
Borrowed from English xylophone; a classical compound (modern coinage), with components derived from Ancient Greek ξύλον (xúlon, “wood”) and φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).
